The Late Wars, 1982–2014

Seven battles from Goose Green in 1982 to Combat Outpost Keating in 2009: the paratroops at Darwin Hill in the Falklands, Eagle Troop at 73 Easting in the Gulf, the crash sites in Mogadishu, the Russian assault on the railway station in Grozny, the Marines and soldiers in Fallujah, and two American outposts in the mountains of north-east Afghanistan, at Wanat and Keating. Every rule is in the Rules; this book holds the armies' figures, the wound tables their battles roll on, and the battlefields.

The battlefields: Darwin Hill 1982, 73 Easting: Eagle Troop crests the rise 1991, Mogadishu: the crash sites 1993, Grozny: the railway station 1995, Fallujah: into the Jolan 2004, Wanat: the patrol base and the observation post 2008, Combat Outpost Keating 2009.

What is switched on

All three modern modules: Modern fire, Armour and mines and Air and night devices, with helicopters, landing by air and thermal sights. The wounded go out by helicopter where a landing zone and a helicopter are left, as the Rules' After the battle says. Wounds heal and fester as the Rules' Recovery says: it does not yet count the antibiotics, the tourniquets or the surgical teams of these wars.

Trouble at work

d10 Trouble
1 An IED or an ambush on the route.
2 The contract is cancelled, and the last month is never paid.
3 His name is on a militia death list.
4 A shooting incident: investigators and lawyers.
5 Kidnapped: the ransom is set at a year's pay.
6 A checkpoint shakedown: pay a bribe or lose the cargo.
7 The employer goes bust, or is banned from the country.
8 A mine strike or an unexploded bomb.
9 A co-worker is skimming or selling information, and he is blamed.
10 The local police arrest him, and his visa is in doubt.

What each skill is for

Skill Use Usually Against Success Failure Fumble
Persuade Haggle: Beat down a price. Ordinary the seller (Persuade) A tenth off (a quarter on a critical). The list price. No sale today.
Persuade Find a billet: Talk a village or a householder into a bed and a meal. Ordinary the householder or headman (Presence) Fed and bedded tonight: no keep to pay. He pays his keep, or sleeps rough. The village turns against the party: trouble.
Persuade Talk past a guard: Get by a sentry, a gate or the provost without the right papers. Hard the sentry or provost (Wits) Through. Turned back. Held as a deserter or a spy.
Persuade Question a prisoner: Get a prisoner or a local to talk. Ordinary the prisoner (Nerve) He tells what he knows (the GM decides how much is true). Nothing. He lies, and is believed.
Command Drive a hard task: Get men to do something hard and tiring: dig all night, march on after dark, cross a river. Ordinary — Done. Done slowly, or only half. They refuse.
Command Keep order: Stop plunder, drinking or a mutinous mood. Hard — They obey. Some slip away to it. They turn on him.
Letters Read or write: Read an order, a letter or a map's names; write a report. Easy — Read or written. Slowly, or with mistakes. He gets it wrong and does not know it.
Letters Forge a pass: Make a pass, an order or a billeting ticket that will be believed. Hard whoever checks it (Watch) It passes. Doubted: Talk past a guard instead. Seen through: held as a deserter or a spy.
Craft Mend kit: Mend a weapon, harness, boots, a cart or a radio set; a day's work. Ordinary — Mended. Not yet: another day. Ruined.
Craft Make something: Make ladders, a raft, a shelter, snowshoes or a litter from what is to hand. Ordinary — Made. Takes twice as long. It fails when it is used.
Drive Drive under pressure: Drive off the road, at night without lights, or under fire. Ordinary — Through. Slowed or lost. Ditched or overturned.
Fieldcraft Track: Follow men or animals. Ordinary the men being followed (Stealth) On their trail. Lost it. On the wrong trail.
Fieldcraft Find the way: Cross country without roads or a guide; at night, hard. Ordinary — On the way. Half a day lost. Lost: a day, or into the enemy.
Fieldcraft Hunt or gather: Find food or water for himself in the country. Ordinary — Fed today: no keep to pay. Nothing found. Something that makes him ill.
Watch Spot: See an ambush, a man hiding, a trap or a thing out of place. Ordinary whoever is hiding (Stealth) Seen. Missed. Sure there is nothing there.
Watch Search: Search a house, a body or a baggage wagon. Easy — Found what there is. Missed it. Missed it and left traces.
Stealth Sneak: Get past sentries, into a camp or away from one. Ordinary the sentries (Watch) Unseen. Seen, but not yet caught. Walks into them.
Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.
Leechcraft Diagnose: Tell what a sick man has, and whether it will spread. Ordinary — Named: the GM tells which sickness. Unsure. Wrong.
Signals Get through: Raise another station, mend a line or a set, or send a message in code. Ordinary — Through. Not yet: try again next hour. The set or line is out until mended.
Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.
Agility Climb or jump: Climb a wall, jump a ditch, keep his feet on ice. Ordinary — Over. Not this way. Falls: roll a fall as a wound.
Endurance Endure: Keep going: swim, go without sleep, hold out in the cold. Ordinary — Holds out. A step of fatigue. Collapses, or goes under.
Wits Notice or remember: Recall a face, a road or a password; work something out. Ordinary — Yes. No. Remembers it wrong.
Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

Wound tables

Each battle rolls its wounds on a table built from the record of that war, and these are the notes on where each one comes from. The tables themselves are in the printed tables and the wound roller. A gameplay-adjusted table is re-weighted from bone evidence to stand for every blow that landed, not only the ones that marked bone; an evidence table is the record itself.

Northern Ireland - penetrating wounds

Primary penetrating wounds, British forces and casualties in Northern Ireland (gunshot and bombs).

How sure: taken directly from a source. Region totals are from the source. The split inside each region uses body exposure (design estimate). Extremities are split 40% arms / 60% legs, the average of the WWII, Korea and Vietnam hospital figures in Neel (1973) Table 7 (design estimate).

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Borden Institute, Weapons Effects and War Wounds, ch. 1, Table 1-2: anatomical distribution of primary penetrating wounds (%): head/neck/face 20, thorax 15, abdomen 15, extremity 50.

Battlefields

Each battlefield lays out on the field map under Battlefield. What follows is what the field and its phases hold, and, briefly, what happened there.

Darwin Hill, Goose Green, 28 May 1982

  • The armies: British and Argentines.
  • Fought for: the crest of Darwin Hill, attacked by the British.
  • The field: 140 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, breeze from the west, dusk.
  • Wounds: Falklands 1982 - penetrating wounds.
  • On the travel map: Goose Green, 1982 (the Darwin isthmus), at Darwin Hill.

What happened

At first light on 28 May 1982 2 Para's A Company was stopped below the Argentine trenches on Darwin Hill and pinned in the gorse gully, B Company on the bare slope to the west. Lieutenant-Colonel H. Jones was killed leading his headquarters against a trench. Later that morning the paratroopers broke into the line with rockets, grenades and machine guns, and by the afternoon they had closed round Goose Green.

How the field is drawn

Darwin Hill at dawn on 28 May 1982, at 10 m a hex: 140 x 110 hexes, about 1400 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: Darwin ridge across the middle with the Argentine trenches along its crest, the gorse gully below Darwin Hill on the right, a gorse hedge across the open slope, Darwin settlement by its inlet of Choiseul Sound in the lower right, Brenton Loch along the left. Light cover (scrub, key o): the gorse in the gully and the gorse hedge, seen and shot through at a cost. The ridge, the gully, the gorse, the shore and the settlement are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the fight at dawn, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Grey first light, a cold westerly, the peat wet underfoot.

73 Easting: Eagle Troop crests the rise, 26 February 1991

  • The armies: Coalition and Iraqis.
  • Fought for: the Iraqi position behind the rise at 73 Easting, attacked by the Coalition.
  • The field: 200 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 2,000 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Sandstorm, strong wind from the north-west.
  • Wounds: Gulf War 1991 (US) - penetrating wounds.
  • On the travel map: 73 Easting, 1991 (the 2nd Armored Cavalry's last day), at the rise at 73 Easting.

What happened

At about 16:20 on 26 February 1991 Eagle Troop, 2nd Armored Cavalry Regiment, came over a low rise in a sandstorm onto a Tawakalna Division tank company dug in on its far side. In about 23 minutes its nine M1A1s and its Bradleys destroyed the position without loss (the accounts give 28 tanks, 16 carriers and about 30 lorries; other tallies differ), then went on to the high ground about 74 Easting and destroyed more T-72s there.

How the field is drawn

The rise at 73 Easting on the afternoon of 26 February 1991, at 10 m a hex: 200 x 120 hexes, about 2 km east to west (from about 72.2 to 74.2 Easting on the military grid) and 1.2 km north to south, north at the top: flat, hard desert, a low rise running north to south across the left middle with the Iraqi trenches and dug-in tanks on its reverse (east) slope, hidden by it (dead ground), and the high ground about 74 Easting on the right. The rise, the trenches and the high ground are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the moment before Eagle Troop crested the rise, just out of the dug-in tanks' sight, in our own words, with round numbers for play. A sandstorm: sight cut to 400 m, thermal sights included (a design choice; in the event the M1A1s' thermal sights saw further than the Iraqis' could), a strong wind. No aircraft fly in it. No minefields are drawn: the accounts we used name none on this ground.

Mogadishu: the crash sites, 3 October 1993

  • The armies: United States and Somali National Alliance.
  • Fought for: Super 61's crash site, attacked by the Somali National Alliance.
  • The field: 110 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,100 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, breeze from the south-west, night.
  • Wounds: Somalia 1993 - penetrating wounds.
  • On the travel map: Mogadishu, 1993 (the airport to the stadium), at Crash site 1 (Super 61).
  • The record: the fight lasted about 783 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

Task Force Ranger landed at the target at about 15:42 and took 24 prisoners. As the force was leaving, Super 61 was shot down by an RPG about three blocks away; the Rangers and Delta fought their way to it on foot and held the houses round it, while Super 64 came down to the south, where two Delta snipers who had asked to go in died defending the crew and the site was overrun. Through the night Little Birds fired for the men at the first crash. At 01:55 the relief column reached them, and at dawn they came out, some of them on foot, to the Pakistani stadium. Eighteen Americans were killed and some 80 wounded; Somali losses are put at 500 to 1,500.

How the field is drawn

The streets round the target and the two crash sites in Mogadishu on the evening of 3 October 1993, at 10 m a hex: 110 x 110 hexes, about 1100 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: the target building left of the middle, the Olympic Hotel down the street from it on Shalalawi Street, the Bakara Market to the south-west, the first crash site to the north-east and the second to the south. The street plan, the houses, the walled yards and the taller buildings are drawn by hand, not traced from any map or photograph: narrow sand streets (open ground), one-storey stone houses behind walls (buildings), the hotel and a few blocks of several storeys (tall buildings), the market's stalls and sheds. The deployment is nightfall, in our own words, with round numbers for play. It is dark (the moon rose late that night); the Little Birds fly at night. The two downed Black Hawks are on the map (downed helicopters). There are no vehicle rules: the relief column can be brought on as infantry from the south with Add a unit.

Grozny: the railway station, 31 December 1994

  • The armies: Russians and Chechens.
  • Fought for: the railway station, attacked by the Chechens.
  • The field: 140 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, calm or light air, dusk.
  • Wounds: Chechnya - penetrating wounds.
  • On the travel map: Grozny, 1995 (the New Year's assault), at Grozny railway station.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 1531 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

On the afternoon of 31 December 1994 the 131st Brigade's 1st Battalion drove into the station square and took the station and the freight yard. Chechen fighters in the buildings round it cut the column off and, through the night, fired rockets down into the tanks and carriers in the streets. Most of the brigade's armour was destroyed, and about 18:00 on 1 January its survivors broke out of the station; Colonel Savin was killed in the breakout (his death is marked on 2 January).

How the field is drawn

The railway station in Grozny at dusk on 31 December 1994, at 10 m a hex: 140 x 110 hexes, about 1400 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: the station building in the middle with its square to the north, the platforms, tracks and freight yard to the south, older houses round the station, and apartment blocks of five and nine storeys beyond, with streets between. The square, station, yards, tracks and blocks are drawn by hand to that pattern, not traced from any map or photograph; the deployment is the fight for the square at dusk, in our own words, with round numbers for play. The apartment blocks are tall buildings (tall buildings), the houses buildings; vehicles keep to the square, the streets and the tracks. Winter dusk, the dark coming on: the phases bring a dark night at about 17:05 (sunset about 16:30, the moon a day from new, worked out for the place and day). The objective is the Chechens': the night was their attack on the station.

Fallujah: into the Jolan, 9 November 2004

  • The armies: Coalition and Insurgents.
  • Fought for: no one place the map can mark.
  • The field: 140 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, breeze from the north-west.
  • Wounds: Iraq & Afghanistan 2001-05 - combat wounds.
  • On the travel map: Fallujah, 2004 (Operation Phantom Fury), at the Jolan.

What happened

The 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines attacked along the river from the evening of 8 November; on 9 November 2004 the 3rd Battalion, 1st Marines came south across the railway into the Jolan behind the tanks and Bradleys of the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry and its own attached Marine tanks, which fired into the houses as they went (McWilliams). The Marines cleared the houses room by room; the insurgents fought from the houses and mosques with rockets, machine guns and snipers and fell back south. By 13 November the Jolan was taken, though the clearing went on for weeks.

How the field is drawn

The northern Jolan in Fallujah on 9 November 2004, at 10 m a hex: 140 x 120 hexes, about 1400 m east to west and 1040 m north to south, north at the top: the apartment blocks and the railway across the top, the Euphrates and its palms down the left, the main street south from the railway, the Jolan's lanes and walled houses everywhere else, the park and four mosques among them. The streets, houses, park, mosques and railway are drawn by hand to that pattern, not traced from any map or photograph; the deployment is the attack south, in our own words, with round numbers for play. The houses are buildings, the blocks and mosques tall buildings; armour keeps to the lanes and the main street. Overcast after the night's rain.

Wanat: the patrol base and the observation post, 13 July 2008

  • The armies: United States and Insurgents.
  • Fought for: Observation Post Topside, attacked by the Insurgents.
  • The field: 90 by 70 hexes of 10 m, about 900 by 610 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air, dusk.
  • Wounds: Iraq & Afghanistan 2001-05 - combat wounds.
  • On the travel map: Wanat, 2008 (the Waygal valley), at Wanat (Vehicle Patrol Base Kahler).

What happened

At about 04:20 some 200 fighters opened fire from the village, the bazaar, the hotel, the mosque, the draw and the high ground, with RPGs and machine guns, on the base and above all on the post, where every man was wounded in the first volley. Men ran from the base up the terraces to hold it; nine Americans were killed, all but one of them at or going to the post, and 27 wounded. Guns from Blessing, Apaches and then jets drove the fighters off after about four hours. The base was given up a few days later.

How the field is drawn

The patrol base and the observation post at Wanat at dawn on 13 July 2008, at 10 m a hex: 90 x 70 hexes, about 900 m east to west and 600 m north to south, north at the top: the base (an open field about 100 m by 300 m) right of the middle, Observation Post Topside on the ridge east of it, the brush-filled draw past the post's north side, the bazaar and hotel to the north, the village and its mosque on the terraces to the west, the Waygal river and the high ground beyond. Light cover (scrub, key o): the brush in the draw, seen and shot through at a cost. The fields, terraces, houses and slopes are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map or photograph; the deployment is about 04:20, in our own words, with round numbers for play. First light (dusk or dawn). The base's barriers were chest-high at best and in places only loose wire: the paratroopers are dug in (gone to ground), the fighters firing from cover. The 120 mm mortar and the TOW were hit in the first minutes; the Apaches came about half an hour in, the jets later.

Combat Outpost Keating, 3 October 2009

  • The armies: Coalition and Insurgents.
  • Fought for: the outpost, attacked by the Insurgents.
  • The field: 120 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,200 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air, dusk.
  • Wounds: Iraq & Afghanistan 2001-05 - combat wounds.
  • On the travel map: COP Keating, 2009 (the Kamdesh valley), at Combat Outpost Keating.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 671 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

At about 06:00 on 3 October 2009 some 300 insurgents opened fire on the outpost from the slopes, pinned the mortar pit, drove the Afghan soldiers back and broke in from the east, setting the buildings alight. The Americans held a line round the barracks and the command post, then counterattacked and took the outpost back by the afternoon, with Apaches and jets striking the slopes. Eight Americans were killed and more than twenty wounded.

How the field is drawn

Combat Outpost Keating at dawn on 3 October 2009, at 10 m a hex: 120 x 110 hexes, about 1200 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: the outpost on its flat in the middle, ringed with wire, the Landay-Sin down the left with the bridge to Urmul, the Kushtoz coming in from the east below the outpost, and steep slopes of rock, scrub and deodar rising on every side. Light cover (scrub, key o): the scrub on the lower slopes among the rock; the deodar above is woods. The flat, the buildings, the river, the stream, the village and the slopes are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map or photograph; the deployment is the attack at dawn, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Observation Post Fritsche, on the ridge to the south-east, is off this field.
